presentingComplaint: Two days of vague upper-abdominal discomfort, nausea and dull lower-back ache, without the classic severe epigastric pain
history: Retired schoolteacher, brought in by his wife for feeling 'not right' — poor appetite, mild constant discomfort across the upper abdomen and a nagging ache in the mid-back that he attributed to his chronic lumbar spondylosis. He denies the sudden severe, boring epigastric pain typically expected; discomfort has been low-grade and gnawing throughout. Two episodes of non-bilious vomiting and reduced oral intake. Drinks around 40 units of alcohol per week for years with a recent binge at a family function 3 days ago. Type 2 diabetic on metformin. No prior similar episodes, no gallstone history. This subtle, pain-light presentation in an older heavy-drinker is easy to mistake for gastritis or a musculoskeletal back complaint.
examination: Alert, mildly uncomfortable but not writhing. Mild epigastric fullness with only modest deep tenderness disproportionately less than the biochemical severity; no guarding or rigidity. Bowel sounds sluggish, mild abdominal distension. No jaundice, no flank ecchymosis. Dry mucous membranes.
imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen: diffusely enlarged, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding and a small amount of free peripancreatic fluid; normal pancreatic enhancement with no necrosis (interstitial oedematous pancreatitis, CT Severity Index low). No gallstones or biliary dilatation. Ultrasound: no cholelithiasis, normal common bile duct.
microbiology: Not applicable — sterile inflammatory process; blood cultures not indicated in the absence of infected necrosis or cholangitis.
finalDiagnosis: Acute (alcohol-related) interstitial oedematous pancreatitis — atypical pain-light presentation, diagnosis secured by lipase >3x ULN plus characteristic CT findings
citations: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) — Management of Acute Pancreatitis — 2013
International Association of Pancreatology / American Pancreatic Association (IAP/APA) — Evidence-based Guidelines for the Management of Acute Pancreatitis — 2013
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis — 2022
stewardship: No antibiotics indicated. Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended in acute pancreatitis, including predicted-severe or sterile necrotising disease; antibiotics are reserved for proven infected necrosis or an extrapancreatic infection (e.g. cholangitis). Management is supportive: goal-directed fluid resuscitation, analgesia, early oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated, and treatment of the precipitant (alcohol cessation, glycaemic control).
contraindications: Avoid empiric prophylactic antibiotics (no survival benefit, promotes resistance and fungal superinfection)
Avoid aggressive over-resuscitation causing volume overload — use moderate goal-directed crystalloid (Ringer's lactate preferred)
Avoid prolonged nil-by-mouth / routine parenteral nutrition when enteral feeding is tolerable
edgeCases: Pain-light or painless pancreatitis in elderly, diabetic, or post-operative patients can lead to missed or delayed diagnosis
Lipase can be normal if presentation is very late; a normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis
Hypertriglyceridaemia and alcohol may coexist as dual precipitants — check triglycerides
Progression to necrotising pancreatitis or organ failure can occur despite an initially benign-appearing exam — reassess with severity scoring
expectedMaiK: Diagnose acute pancreatitis by the revised Atlanta criteria (2 of 3: characteristic pain, lipase/amylase >3x ULN, or cross-sectional imaging) even when the pain is atypical/subtle, and manage supportively without antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: Alcohol quantity and timing of last binge?
Any gallstone disease or prior biliary symptoms?
Current medications and recent new drugs (drug-induced pancreatitis)?
Any features of organ failure (urine output, breathlessness, confusion)?
expectedInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT / abdominal ultrasound for gallstones and biliary duct
Renal function, CRP and severity scoring (BISAP / revised Atlanta)
regressionAssertions: Engine must identify pancreatitis as top diagnosis despite atypical pain-light presentation
Diagnosis rests on lipase >3x ULN plus CT findings (revised Atlanta), not on pain severity
No antibiotics should be recommended (prophylaxis contraindicated in acute pancreatitis)
Differential should include peptic ulcer, biliary colic, cholecystitis and mesenteric ischaemia
